intro: Elgar gives Isabel Fitton, his viola pupil, a portrait built from a string-crossing exercise. The awkward leap becomes a tender melody for her own instrument.

sections.label: Var 6 · Isabel’s viola exercise
sections.mNote: The bow crosses strings; the phrase opens into song

cues.title: A bow crosses strings
cues.text: The violas’ opening figure dips low and leaps back up across the strings. A long note follows the leap, giving the phrase room to sing. Bassoons and clarinets answer in little fragments while the violas keep returning to their exercise.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 31–34, rehearsal figures 19–22. Elgar identifies the recurring opening phrase as a string-crossing exercise in My Friends Pictured Within, section VI. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/1e/IMSLP23792-PMLP07276-Elgar_-_Enigma_Variations_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Isabel brings her viola
cues.text: Isabel Fitton belongs to a musical family in Malvern and studies viola with Elgar. Crossing from one string to another is a beginner’s difficulty he knows from teaching. For her portrait he takes that small piece of daily practice and builds an entire Andantino around it.
cues.evidence: Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello), section VI: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/06/IMSLP339677-SIBLEY1802.27173.6d2a-39087004945996text.pdf. Fitton’s family and viola playing: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm. Her lessons with Elgar: Max Raimi, Chicago Symphony, 9 July 2025, https://cso.org/experience/article/24910/elgar-and-his-close-circle-of-friends-immorta

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 31–34, rehearsal figures 19–22: Variation VI, Ysobel, with its string-crossing figure and solo viola.

timeline.note: The violas begin their string-crossing figure as the low-brass chord from the preceding variation dies away (p. 31).
Flutes and horns join the phrase, and the viola line becomes a solo. Bassoons answer with small rising figures (pp. 31–32).
The solo viola sings molto cantabile, with clarinet and bassoon replies. Second violins add a few plucked notes (p. 32).
The first violins rise above the viola melody. Oboes join the woodwinds, and a brief timpani roll supports the phrase (p. 33).
A horn holds a soft note while a solo viola recalls the opening leap. The cellos close with a quiet chord (p. 34).

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
